podcast.title: Tire Warehouse Recording
podcast.body: Released in 2000, this album was recorded in an abandoned tire warehouse they rented for $500 a month, using only used gear and recycled recording tape. The album's title reflects its unconventional recording location. "Their 2000 album was entitled, Surprise, Rubber Factory, makes sense."

podcast.body: The third album was recorded over five months in an abandoned General Tire factory in East Akron, Ohio, which ceased operations in 1982. The band rented the second floor for $500 a month, acquired a recording console on eBay that was previously owned by a sound engineer for Loverboy (though it proved to be "crap" and was abandoned post-recording), and utilized recycled recording tape. Despite technical glitches, the album garnered positive reviews, led to a slot at Lollapalooza, and an appearance on David Letterman. It was their first album to break into the top 200 album chart, peaking at number 143. "The third album was recorded in a different spot, an abandoned tire factory in East Akron that was once run by General Tyre, but they bailed out in 1982."

podcast.body: The third album, recorded over five months in the second floor of a former General Tire factory in East Akron, Ohio, rented for $500 a month. The band used a recording console bought on eBay (once owned by a Loverboy sound engineer, but deemed "crap") and recycled, baked recording tape provided by their label. Despite glitches with the space and gear, it received good reviews, secured a slot at Lollapalooza, a performance on David Letterman, and was their first album to break into the Top 200 album chart, peaking at number 143. "In the end, they called it, what else, rubber factory."
